Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Ceres, Head of ML), Tom Wu (Ceres, Platform Engineer), Priya Nair (Ceres, Security)
Recording: https://app.fireflies.ai/recordings/ff-20260304-ceres-001 (auto-generated)

Summary: quick discovery focused on migrating from OpenAI-hosted endpoints to Redwood Dedicated. Covered compatibility concerns (vLLM/TGI), eval parity, perf/latency tradeoffs, security (KMS/SOC2/SSO), and next steps for benchmarks and pricing.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um this is Maya from Redwood. We also have Samir on the line, our solutions engineer. How's it going?
[00:04] Lena Ortiz: Hi Maya, thanks. We've been long overdue to talk about migration, so excited to hear what you have.
[00:07] Samir Patel: Great, hi Lena, hi Tom, hi Priya. Quick agenda — understand current setup, pain points, compatibility questions, and outline a pilot path.
[00:15] Tom Wu: Briefly, we're currently on OpenAI "org"-managed endpoints; cost has spiked with the last quarter, and latency can be unpredictable for our real-time flows. We're also experimenting with vLLM on prem for some workloads.
[00:28] Priya Nair: From security, main things are data residency, SOC2 certs, SSO/SAML, and KMS integration for key management and audit logs.
[00:36] Maya Chen: Makes sense. Can you say a bit about volume and latency SLOs?
[00:40] Lena Ortiz: We're doing a mix. For chat assistants — 5k qps peak across shards? Maybe that's high; currently about 2000 requests per minute, spikes to 6-7k/min during business hours. Latency SLO for UI responses is 300ms p50, 1s p95. Cost per 1M tokens is a major trigger to consider dedicated.
[01:00] Samir Patel: Helpful. Quick note: Redwood Dedicated is our reserved capacity offering — predictable throughput, private pools, and you can pin model versions. We run GPU-optimized runtime, continuous batching, and prefix caching which can drive down per-token cost.
[01:15] Tom Wu: Two immediate questions: 1) Will our prompts/evals run exactly the same on Redwood as OpenAI? We built a lot of prompt engineering around OpenAI idiosyncrasies. 2) How compatible is Redwood with vLLM/TGI tooling we already use?
[01:28] Samir Patel: On eval parity — there's no one-to-one guarantee because different model weights and tokenizers can change outputs. That said, we support multiple open models in our catalog and provide evaluation harnesses so you can run A/B parity tests — side-by-side generation with your golden prompts. We also support model variants and pinned versions to reduce drift.
[01:45] Lena Ortiz: So we can bring our prompt sets and get an apples-to-apples comparison?
[01:48] Samir Patel: Yes, exactly. We'll run your canonical prompts through Redwood-hosted models and through whichever baseline you have (OpenAI), and produce a quality/latency/cost matrix. We also have tooling to simulate production load.
[01:59] Priya Nair: For compliance, do you provide customer-managed keys?
[02:02] Maya Chen: Yes, for Dedicated and Private we support KMS integrations, HSM options for on-prem, and audit logs. We'll share the security whitepaper and SOC2 artifacts.
[02:12] Tom Wu: Cool. About vLLM/TGI — we use vLLM in our staging to squeeze latency for smaller Llama-ish models. How does Redwood compare if we were to keep vLLM in the loop?
[02:22] Samir Patel: vLLM is great for certain workloads; note though vLLM and TGI implementations vary — kernel selection, batch strategy, KV cache behavior. Our runtime is optimized at the kernel and serving layer; in internal benchmarks we've seen better throughput at lower tail latency for the same instance class compared to vanilla vLLM setups, but results depend on model, sequence length, and batch patterns. We'll share the benchmark template and sample results.
[02:45] Lena Ortiz: When you say better tail latency — are we talking p95 improvements of tens to hundreds of ms?
[02:49] Samir Patel: Tens of ms on typical chat lengths, can be more for long seqs because of KV cache management. But again, depends on batching and caching patterns.
[02:58] Tom Wu: Another operational question: how do model rollouts work? We need canary, A/B, and auto-fallback to hosted fallback if Dedicated capacity is constrained.
[03:07] Maya Chen: We support canary and A/B rollouts via the Redwood Console; you can set routing policies by latency/cost/region, and automatic fallback to a compatible variant, including an OpenAI-hosted fallback if you want hybrid mode.
[03:18] Priya Nair: Hybrid mode sounds interesting, but it raises data flow questions — what leaves our VPC?
[03:22] Samir Patel: For Private deployments, control plane is customer-managed; with Dedicated we can restrict egress and route logs to your logging collector. We'll detail the network flow diagrams — egress only to model artifact storage if needed, and we support VPC peering and private links.
[03:36] Lena Ortiz: Cost modeling — can you share the levers? We currently use batching on our side with vLLM; what additional knobs do we get?
[03:44] Samir Patel: Batching, prefix/KV caching (saves tokens for repeat prompts), quantization profiles (int8/4) where quality vs speed tradeoffs are transparent, and routing policies to send non-critical requests to cheaper variants. Redwood Optimize suggests configs per workload.
[04:01] Tom Wu: About quantization — do you support running the same model in multiple quantization profiles and measure quality regressions?
[04:07] Samir Patel: Yes, we do quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to your prompt sets, so we can run comparisons and flag regressions automatically.
[04:15] Lena Ortiz: Great. Let's talk migration path — minimum viable pilot?
[04:18] Maya Chen: Typical pilot: you provide 3-5 canonical prompts + traffic profile; we do a week-long parity eval under your load shape using our Dedicated test pool; we provide a report comparing latency, cost, and quality. If that looks good, we do a 30-day pilot with a few routes migrated and monitoring.
[04:33] Lena Ortiz: About data retention — logs, transcripts, payloads — how long do you keep them? We need to meet a 90-day retention policy and ability to purge on demand.
[04:41] Maya Chen: We have retention controls per customer, and Dedicated/Private offer shorter default retention. We also can set automatic purge and support on-demand purge for logs; we'll include this in the security docs.
[04:50] Tom Wu: Any concerns with tokenization differences? We've seen models tokenize punctuation differently which can change prompt engineering results.
[04:56] Samir Patel: Tokenization differences are real. Best approach is to run your prompt set and compare, and if needed we can recommend model variants with closer tokenizers. Also supporting aliases in the SDK to normalize inputs is something our SDK team recommends.
[05:09] Priya Nair: On SOC2 and ISO, we're regulated. Can you share the scope, and do you allow us to audit?
[05:15] Maya Chen: We can share SOC2 reports under NDA and work with you on scope. For Dedicated and Private customers, we provide additional logs and support audits.
[05:23] Tom Wu: If we move to Dedicated, what's the support SLA and escalation path during a live incident?
[05:28] Maya Chen: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed targets for uptime and latency tiers depending on the contract. We provide 24/7 on-call for P1s and a designated TAM for enterprise customers.
[05:36] Lena Ortiz: Good. Regarding software stack, how do your client SDKs integrate with our existing orchestrator? We have router and throttling logic in k8s.
[05:44] Samir Patel: We have REST and gRPC SDKs; many customers run a thin sidecar in K8s that handles retries, backoff, and local batching. For Dedicated we provide private endpoints and VPC peering.
[05:55] Tom Wu: For the eval, Samir, can you run a load that simulates our 6k/min spikes? If we see the same tail behavior as OpenAI we'll be worried.
[06:02] Samir Patel: Yep, we'll mirror your spikes in staging. Please include typical prompt length and session lengths in the profile.
[06:09] Lena Ortiz: One more — what about support for Anthropic model parity? We're evaluating Anthropic for certain safety-sensitive flows.
[06:16] Samir Patel: We have Anthropic models in our catalog in hosted mode; for Dedicated customers we can bring Anthropic weights where licensing allows or provide compatible open models. We'll map out the options for safety-sensitive routes.
[06:27] Priya Nair: Compliance question — do logs include PII? We need token redaction before logs persist.
[06:33] Maya Chen: We support customizable redaction rules and can redact tokens before logs are stored. We'll include the redaction options in the security doc.
[06:42] Tom Wu: Ok wrapping up, can you outline the concrete next steps?
[06:45] Maya Chen: Sure. We'll: 1) send Dedicated pricing + architecture diagram, 2) Samir will share benchmark harness and example vLLM vs Redwood numbers, 3) Ceres provides canonical prompts and traffic profile, 4) schedule a tech deep dive with infra.
[06:58] Lena Ortiz: Sounds good. Priya, any blockers from your side?
[07:01] Priya Nair: Need to review security docs and ensure KMS/HSM options meet our compliance. After that I think we're fine with pilot.
[07:07] Maya Chen: Great, we'll get docs over. Thanks everyone.
[07:11] Tom Wu: Thanks, talk soon.
[07:13] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription quality: auto transcript shows occasional mis-hearings (e.g., "KV cash" instead of KV cache, "Redwood Dedi" typed once). Speakers occasionally overlap; timestamps are approximate.
